source.title: Tensor Network Machine Learning for Wildfire Susceptibility Mapping: from Grokking Dynamics to Quantum Mixedness of Class Representations
source.authors: Domenico Pomarico; A. Costantino; Gabriel Ramirez Sanchez; L. Bellantuono; Davide D' Alò; M. Elia; A. Fania; Francesco Giordano; N. Kheirkhahan; R. Lafortezza; E. Pantaleo; S. Tangaro; R. Bellotti; Alfonso Monaco; N. Amoroso

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests grokking-like training dynamics in a new, non-algorithmic setting: an MPS classifier trained for wildfire susceptibility mapping from geospatial embeddings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own binary and multiclass training trajectories and internal magnetization dynamics. Grokking results cited from other work are not recorded as findings here.
record.test_reason: The paper reports its own training trajectories for an MPS classifier on non-algorithmic geospatial wildfire data. In the binary task, test accuracy and sensitivity jump late (about 400–600 sweeps) with no matching discontinuity in training accuracy. That bears on the non-algorithmic-data part of V3. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also interpret the binary jump as a reorganization from a memorization-dominated regime to structure-capturing generalization, which they did not directly measure. They attribute the binary/multiclass difference to task structure, although the two tasks used different bond dimensions and learning rates.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an MPS classifier on geospatial wildfire susceptibility data and AlphaEarth embeddings, rather than the original small algorithmic-task setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported dynamics differ between the binary and four-class formulations: the binary task has a sharp transition, while multiclass improvement is broader and class-dependent. Initialization scale and weight norm are not varied.

fits_no_version.finding: Pauli σZ magnetization patterns of the MPS quantum mask stabilize into bands at the time of the grokking transition. Their across-run standard deviation peaks near the transition (about 7e-2 binary, 8e-2 multiclass) and then decays.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Internal representation statistics of the model reorganize and stabilize concurrently with a delayed-generalization jump.

record.problems: The reported grokking evidence is from one wildfire mapping setting, not algorithmic datasets. The paper does not state that training accuracy has saturated before the test jump, report chance-level test accuracy, or test initialization/weight-norm effects. Trajectory values are primarily described in text and plotted; uncertainty is based on three independent runs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant trajectory results were omitted.

untested.parts: No small algorithmic datasets are used, and training-set size is not varied.
No generalizing circuit is identified and removal of memorizing components is not measured. No continuous measure is shown to anticipate the jump; magnetization is only said to coincide with it.
The on/off switch through initialization scale, weight norm or a lazy-to-rich transition is not tested.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning is studied.
Weight decay, norm, critical dataset size and ungrokking are not tested.
Algorithms are not compared across runs, architectures or hyperparameters.
Optimizer and numerical controls are absent. Training uses mini-batch SGD with per-sweep renormalization and SVD truncation, and these are never varied.

missing.what: Final test metrics: binary accuracy 87.07%, sensitivity 91.13%, specificity 83.02%; multiclass accuracy 53.01% with per-class 75.47/35.88/38.21/62.49%. These show the post-transition level is not near-perfect.

record.verdict_notes: There is a single region and dataset, with three runs. Uncertainty bands are only plotted. 'Grokking' here means a delayed jump while training accuracy is still rising; saturation is never stated and chance level is not given. The study cites the authors' own prior MPS grokking papers (refs 14, 15) as interpretive support, not as results. The 20/30/40-feature benchmark results are selection values and correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses wildfire susceptibility data, not small algorithmic datasets such as modular arithmetic tables; it does not test the claimed training-set-size effect.

It monitors MPS magnetization patterns during training, but does not identify a Fourier or other explicit algorithm, measure removal of memorizing components, or show that a continuous progress measure anticipates the test-accuracy jump.
The study tests grokking-like dynamics on geospatial wildfire data, but does not vary initialization scale or weight norm or test a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning is studied.
The study does not test weight decay, low-norm efficiency, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
Three independent runs are reported, but the study does not compare identifiable algorithms learned across runs or vary architecture and hyperparameters to test convergence to the same algorithm.
The study does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point limits in the softmax, or control these as explanations of the delay.

rows.subject: MPS classifier, binary classification
rows.operation_detail: Trained on the binary wildfire task, class 0 versus aggregated classes 1–3; training trajectory evaluated over sweeps.
rows.baseline: Early test performance is described as significantly lower than training performance; chance level not stated.
rows.value: A sharp test-accuracy jump occurs approximately between 400 and 600 sweeps; performance then stabilizes at high values with a small generalization gap.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over three independent runs, shown as shaded regions; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The authors describe this binary trajectory as a grokking-like delayed, abrupt gain in generalization on non-algorithmic geospatial data.
rows.check: The baseline is not a chance level. Training accuracy is described as still increasing, not saturated, when the jump occurs. The final binary test accuracy is 87.07% (Table 1), so performance stabilizes 'high', not near-perfect.

source_check.locator_found: Results, Figure 2 caption and accompanying discussion, pp. 4–5.

rows.subject: MPS classifier, binary classification
rows.operation_detail: Training accuracy tracked over sweeps during binary wildfire classification.
rows.value: Training accuracy increases steadily; the test-accuracy jump has no corresponding discontinuity in training performance.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over three independent runs, shown as shaded regions; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The text does not explicitly state when training accuracy saturates.
rows.check: This is context for R1, not an effect row. It only says training accuracy rises steadily, and never states when or whether it saturates. So it cannot show that training saturated before the test jump; 'partial' is not a readable state.

source_check.locator_found: Results, binary training dynamics accompanying Figure 2, p. 5.

rows.subject: MPS classifier, binary classification
rows.operation_detail: Test sensitivity tracked over sweeps during binary wildfire classification.
rows.baseline: Sensitivity is described as suppressed before the transition; chance level not stated.
rows.value: Sensitivity remains suppressed until approximately 400–600 sweeps, then rises sharply and rapidly aligns with the training curve.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over three independent runs, shown as shaded regions; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: Specificity rises more rapidly than sensitivity in the early phase, according to the text.
rows.check: None beyond the missing numeric values. They are read from the text describing Figure 2.

source_check.locator_found: Results, Figure 2 caption, p. 4; sensitivity transition discussion, p. 5.

rows.subject: MPS classifier, four-class classification
rows.operation_detail: Trained on the four-class wildfire task; test performance tracked over sweeps.
rows.baseline: Early test performance is described as low and unstable; chance level not stated.
rows.value: Performance improves rapidly but unevenly across classes over a broader range of sweeps; the authors describe the multiclass transition as distributed rather than a single sharp jump.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over three independent runs, shown as shaded regions; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The authors describe the multiclass dynamics as hierarchical and class-dependent.
rows.check: The multiclass run used different hyperparameters from the binary run (bond dimension 500 vs 1000, learning rate 7e-4 vs 5e-3). Binary-versus-multiclass differences are therefore confounded with optimizer settings, not only task structure. Final multiclass test accuracy is 53.01%.

source_check.locator_found: Results, multiclass dynamics accompanying Figure 2, pp. 5–6; Methods, p. 11.

rows.subject: MPS classifier, four-class classification
rows.operation_detail: Class-wise test accuracy tracked over sweeps.
rows.measure: Class 0 test accuracy over training sweeps
rows.baseline: Early class-wise test accuracy is described as low and unstable; chance level not stated.
rows.value: Class 0 approaches values near 80% relatively quickly.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over three independent runs, shown as shaded regions; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The text does not give a precise sweep at which class 0 reaches the stated level.
rows.check: Class 0 is described as reaching about 80% 'relatively quickly', so this class shows no delayed jump. Table 1 gives the final class 0 accuracy as 75.47%.

source_check.locator_found: Results, class-wise trajectory discussion, p. 6; Table 1, p. 5.

rows.subject: MPS classifier, four-class classification
rows.operation_detail: Class-wise test accuracy tracked over sweeps.
rows.measure: Class-wise test accuracy over training sweeps
rows.baseline: Early class-wise test accuracy is described as low and unstable; chance level not stated.
rows.value: Classes 1, 2, and 3 plateau at substantially lower levels, typically between 40% and 60%.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over three independent runs, shown as shaded regions; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The text reports this range for classes 1–3 collectively, not separate values for each class.
rows.check: The text says classes 1–3 plateau at 40–60%. Table 1's final values are 35.88% (class 1), 38.21% (class 2) and 62.49% (class 3), so the text range is inconsistent with the table. Generalization stays far from near-perfect.

source_check.locator_found: Results, class-wise trajectory discussion, p. 6; Table 1, p. 5.

rows.subject: MPS classifier, binary classification
rows.operation_detail: Tracked Pauli σZ expectation values across feature sites and training sweeps.
rows.value: After an initial transient, horizontal bands emerge and stabilize; the pattern is described as coinciding temporally with the grokking transition. The standard deviation has a single peak of approximately 7 × 10−2 in the class-0 mask near the transition, followed by rapid decay toward negligible values.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over three independent runs; peak approximately 7 × 10−2.
rows.note: The paper treats magnetization as a proxy for feature activation; it does not establish that the measure anticipates the accuracy jump or that memorizing components are removed.
rows.check: Magnetization is a feature-activation proxy, not an identified generalizing circuit or memorization measure. It is reported only as coinciding with the transition, not anticipating it. It belongs under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: MPS classifier, four-class classification
rows.operation_detail: Tracked class-wise Pauli σZ expectation values across feature sites and training sweeps.
rows.value: The class-0 pattern is described as nearly reproducing the binary class-0 pattern; patterns for classes 1, 2, and 3 resemble the binary aggregate classes 1–3 pattern, with lower amplitudes and more diffuse appearance. The standard deviation has a single peak of approximately 8 × 10−2 in the class-0 mask near the transition, followed by rapid decay toward negligible values.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over three independent runs; peak approximately 8 × 10−2.
rows.note: These internal patterns are reported as representation structure, but the paper does not identify an explicit algorithm or measure removal of memorizing components.
rows.check: This row compares representation structure across task formulations. No algorithm is identified, removal of memorizing components is not measured, and no anticipation of the jump is shown. It belongs under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Binary MPS wildfire classification (class 0 vs 1–3), AlphaEarth embeddings, three runs
relationships.reason: Test accuracy and sensitivity stay low, then jump at about 400–600 sweeps with no training discontinuity (R1, R3). Training saturation is not shown, and the final test accuracy is 87%.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy and sensitivity jumped around 400–600 sweeps without a training discontinuity, reaching 87% final accuracy, although training saturation was unestablished.

relationships.condition: Four-class MPS wildfire classification (different bond dimension and learning rate)
relationships.reason: There is no single sharp jump (R4). Class 0 is learned quickly with no delay (R5), and classes 1–3 plateau at roughly 36–62% (R6).
relationships.display_finding: There was no single sharp jump: class 0 learned quickly without delay, while classes 1–3 plateaued at roughly 36–62%.
